newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's aspiring king tries to rally support.
newsitem.headline: Albania's aspiring king tries to rally support.

text.p: Albania's self-proclaimed King Leka I went back on tour on Wednesday to keep alive his campaign to restore the monarchy after a referendum in the chaotic Balkan nation rejected the throne.

As numbers at daily monarchist rallies in Tirana dwindle, Leka headed north to Shkoder, the only major town of Albania where the monarchists and supporters of President Sali Berisha's ousted right-wing Democratic Party still rule.
Up to 2,000 people gathered under the blazing, midday sun to hail the would-be king, waving Albania's red and black flag and holding their thumbs and index fingers in an "L" salute.
"Without the monarchy there will be no peace in Albania," Leka told the cheering crowd, flanked by his heavily armed posse of bodyguards and police in riot gear.

Leka, 58, arrived in Albania from his South African home in April amid a violent rebellion sparked by the collapse of popular savings funds in which over 1,500 have died. This forced the Democratic government to resign and a new election.

He is laying claim to the throne in Europe's poorest nation, left vacant since his father, King Zog I, fled Albania in 1939, before Mussolini's troops invaded. He was barred from the country during the communist era that ended in 1990.
Early results of the referendum, held alongside the election on June 29, showed 66 percent opposed to restoring the monarchy. Final results were due to be released this week.

But Leka claims the referendum was manipulated and has pledged to continue his fight for the throne -- backed by the Democrats who were crushed in the election by the reformed ex-communist Socialists in all areas but Shkoder.
"You have seen that Fatos Nano (leader of the Socialists) has cheated us," said Leka, whose campaign promise was that the monarchy was above party politics.
"Please protect your vote but in a peaceful way," urged the aspiring royal who at 2.04 metres (six feet eight inches) tall towers above most of his 3.4 million countrymen.
Support for the would-be king was still running high in Shkoder, one of the country's largest towns that lies in the mountainous north, about 110 kms from the capital Tirana.

Leka's popularity appeared to be waning in Tirana after a rally of monarchists last Thursday attended by several leading Democrats erupted in violence, with one man shot dead and several others injured.

"He is the saviour of our nation," said Shkoder housewife Lale Ftoni of Leka, who was expelled from Spain after the discovery of an arms cache at his home outside Madrid and spent five days in a Thai jail on illegal weapons charges.
"The political parties will take the country into chaos and only the king can save us."
Salesman Sytki Halili said the townsfolk had accepted the Democrats losing the election but were still hoping Leka would become king.
"The king is above politics. We are hoping for something out of him," Halili said.
"It is relatively calm now after the months of violence but people are worried that at any time this could be disrupted again by politics and our lives made worse."
